title: Stone Game VIII
statement:
A row of stones has values `stones` (left to right, values may be negative). Alice and Bob alternate turns, and Alice moves first. As long as the row holds two or more stones, the player whose turn it is must:

- pick a whole number `x` with `x >= 2` (and at most the current number of stones),
- take away the `x` leftmost stones and add their total value to their own score,
- put one new stone whose value is that same total at the left end of the row.

Play stops as soon as a single stone remains. Alice tries to make (Alice's score minus Bob's score) as large as possible, and Bob tries to make it as small as possible. Return that difference when both of them play perfectly.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating the game is exponential. The key observation is that the new stone always holds the sum of every original stone removed so far, so after any move the leftmost stone equals a prefix sum `prefix[k]` of the original row, and the mover scores exactly `prefix[k]`. A move is therefore just a choice of a new end index `k` that is past the previous one, and the whole state is that last index.

Let `f(i)` be the best difference the player to move can force when they may end at any index `k >= i`. Ending exactly at `i` gives `prefix[i] - f(i + 1)`, since the opponent then faces the same game from `i + 1`; ending later is worth `f(i + 1)`. So `f(i) = max(f(i + 1), prefix[i] - f(i + 1))`.

## Approach

1. Build `prefix`, where `prefix[i]` is the sum of `stones[0..i]`.
2. At the last index the mover must take everything, so start `best = prefix[n - 1]`.
3. Walk `i` from `n - 2` down to `1`, updating `best = max(best, prefix[i] - best)`.
4. The first move removes at least two stones, so its end index is at least `1`; return `best`, which is `f(1)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`stones = [-1, 2, -3, 4, -5]` gives `prefix = [-1, 1, -2, 2, -3]`.

- Start: `best = -3`.
- `i = 3`: `max(-3, 2 - (-3)) = 5`.
- `i = 2`: `max(5, -2 - 5) = 5`.
- `i = 1`: `max(5, 1 - 5) = 5`.

The answer is `5`: Alice ends at index 3 (scoring 2) and Bob must take the rest (scoring -3).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass for the prefix sums and one pass for the recurrence.
- Space: O(n) for `prefix` (it could reuse `stones` for O(1) extra).

## Pitfalls

- Stop the loop at `i = 1`, not `0`: a first move that ends at index 0 would take a single stone, which is illegal.
- A player cannot pass, so even a negative `prefix` value may be forced; never clamp scores at 0.
- `best` already stands for the opponent's reply, so subtract it, do not add it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of stones |
| `prefix` | `prefix[i]` = sum of `stones[0..i]` |
| `i` | the earliest index the mover may end their take at |
| `best` | `f(i)`: the best difference the mover can force from index `i` on |

narration.3: prefix[i] will hold the total of stones 0 through i, which is the merged stone after a move ending at i.
narration.5: Extend the running sums one stone at a time.
narration.6: Each prefix sum adds one more stone to the previous one.
narration.8: Ending at the last index takes every stone and ends the game, so that is the base value.
narration.9: Work backwards over the earlier end indices; index 0 is excluded because a move takes at least two stones.
narration.10: Either end later (keep best) or end here, gaining prefix[i] while the opponent gets best from the next index.
narration.12: best now covers every legal first move, so it is Alice's optimal difference.
